scenarios.name: fix-async-fixture-strict-mode
scenarios.rationale: Both name the strict-mode cause, show `@pytest_asyncio.fixture` with `import pytest_asyncio`, and mention `asyncio_mode = auto` as an alternative without telling the user to rewrite the fixture synchronously; A is more focused, while B adds extra loop_scope and version advice that goes beyond the question.

scenarios.name: configure-pytest-toml-with-markers
scenarios.rationale: Both fix imports with pythonpath, set asyncio_mode auto, register the slow marker, show strict marker enforcement, and run `pytest -m "not slow"`; A uses `strict = true` (matches the rubric exactly, though it needs pytest 9 and `pytest.toml`), while B uses `--strict-markers` via addopts (an accepted equivalent) and adds useful extras like the ini variant and a default-skip option.

scenarios.name: mock-email-patch-lookup-location
scenarios.rationale: Response A matches the rubric: it uses the pytest-mock `mocker` fixture, patches `app.services.notifications.send_email` with `new_callable=AsyncMock` and a `return_value`, asserts with `assert_awaited_once_with`, and checks the returned id. Response B patches the definition site `app.services.email.send_email`, uses `unittest.mock.patch` instead of `mocker`, and claims the notifications path would raise `AttributeError`, so it contradicts the rubric on the central requirement.
